title: The Night It Snowed in the Desert
summary: In a village where it never snows, Amira dreams of seeing real snow. And one winter afternoon, the wind changes direction.

scenes.text:
In Pozo de Luna, the village where Amira lived, it was always hot.

The stones kept hold of the sun until midnight. The earth smelled of warm dust and freshly baked bread. And the cacti, as tall as grandpas, gazed out at the desert without moving.

At night, Amira slept on the porch, with a wet cloth on her forehead. At the foot of the bed slept Canela, the family dog.

And under her pillow, Amira kept a treasure: a page torn out of an old magazine.

In the picture there was a white street, white rooftops, trees with sugar on their branches.

Snow.

Amira had never seen snow. Nobody in the village had ever seen it. That's why she dreamed about it almost every night.

"Grandpa," she said that night, "is snow really cold?"

Grandpa Simón was sitting in his wooden chair, fanning himself with his hat.

"Cold as water from the well," he said. "Cold and soft at the same time. And when you squeeze it in your hand, it crunches."

Amira looked at him with narrowed eyes.

"And how do you know, Grandpa? It never snows here."

Grandpa was quiet for a long while. That long while when grown-ups go looking for a memory they've kept tucked away.

"Because it snowed here once," he said slowly. "A hundred years ago. And my grandma was there."

"She was six, nearly the same as you," said Grandpa. "It was a January night. An icy air came down from the mountains, and people took the blankets out of their trunks without understanding a thing.

"And then the sky turned white.

"Something was falling that wasn't rain, and wasn't dust. It fell slowly, as if the sky were pulling the petals off an enormous flower.

"The whole village came out into the square in their pyjamas. The children filled their pockets with snow to keep it.

"My grandma filled a jar and put it under her bed. The next morning there was only water left, and she cried.

"But she remembered that night every day of her life. And that's why I'm telling it to you."

The next day, Amira got out her pencils and drew the snowfall from a hundred years ago.

She drew the village from above: the church, the well, the rooftops, Doña Rosalía's bakery. And then she coloured it all in white, with a worn-down pencil, pressing hard.

She put little white dots in the air. Lots of them. Hundreds. Thousands.

The white pencil ended up the size of a bean.

Higo, the family cat, jumped onto the table and sat right on top of the drawing, the way cats always do.

"Move, Higo," laughed Amira. "You're sitting in the square."

That night she stuck the drawing on the wall, next to the window. And before she went to sleep, she spoke to it in a whisper:

"One day I'm going to see you for real."

The days went by, and Amira learned to watch the sky the way grown-ups do.

Grandpa taught her the names of the clouds. The fat ones, which bring nothing. The ones with grey tummies, which sometimes do. The ones that race along very high up, just passing through.

He taught her to lick her finger and hold it up, to find out which way the air was coming from.

"What if it snows while I'm asleep?" Amira would ask.

"Then I'll wake you up," Grandpa promised. "A grandpa's promise."

And then, one winter afternoon, something strange happened.

Amira was sweeping the porch when she felt a shiver on her arms. She looked up. She licked her finger and held it up, the way Grandpa had taught her.

The air wasn't coming warm from the desert any more. It was coming down from the mountains, thin and icy.

It had changed direction, the wind.

The washing on the line puffed out like the sails of a ship. The sky turned a colour Amira had never seen: grey with a little bit of violet, like the inside of a shell.

Grandpa came out into the yard without his hat. He sniffed the air slowly, and didn't say a word.

But his eyes were shining.

The animals knew before the people did.

Canela, who never came into the house, crept under Amira's bed, trembling, and from there she kept barking at the window.

The hens squashed together in one corner of the yard, until they looked like one big warm hen. Higo climbed onto the clay oven and stayed there, on the warm part, curled up in a ring.

Even the ants blocked the entrance to their nest with tiny pebbles.

"Grandpa, why is everything so strange?"

"Because something's coming," said Grandpa, putting a blanket round her shoulders. "The animals can smell it. All we can do is wait."

That night, the household went to bed early, because the cold made everyone sleepy.

Not Amira. Amira stayed awake, with her nose pressed against the windowpane, wrapped in two blankets, looking at the empty street. The lamp on the corner made a circle of yellow light on the ground.

Her eyes kept closing. She breathed on the glass to mist it up, and drew a little house with smoke with her finger.

And at that very moment, into the circle of light from the lamp, something came down.

It came down slowly, turning, in no hurry at all. It was small and white, and as it crossed the light, it sparkled.

It was a snowflake.

Behind it came another. And another. And another.

It was snowing in Pozo de Luna.

Amira ran out of her room, barefoot.

"Grandpa! Grandpa, Grandpa, GRANDPA!"

She banged on his door with both hands.

It opened, and there he was, with his white hair all messy and his eyes small with sleep.

"What is it, my girl?"

"It's falling! From the sky! White!"

Grandpa didn't ask anything else. He pulled on his boots without socks, grabbed the blanket off his bed and followed her out.

Amira woke her mum. She woke her dad. She woke her little brother, who was sleeping with his mouth open.

And the whole family went out into the yard in their pyjamas, to look at the sky.

In Pozo de Luna, news doesn't need a telephone.

First one window lit up. Then another. Then, all along the street, the houses opened up, one by one.

Out of every house came people in pyjamas, with coats on top, with blankets, with woolly hats nobody had ever worn.

At first nobody spoke loudly. There were only whispers, like in church. The square was changing colour: the ground was turning white, the rooftops were turning white, and the edge of the well had a little hat of snow.

Even a little desert fox came out of its den to look, with its enormous ears.

And then the baker opened his mouth to catch snow on his tongue. And somebody laughed. And from one end of the village to the other, the laughter spread.

What happened next, Amira never forgot.

The whole village began to play, in the middle of the night.

The children ran down the middle of the street, leaving footprints and stepping on them again. Under their shoes, the snow made a new and perfect sound: crick!

That night, Amira learned that you can catch snow on your tongue, that it melts in your hand, and that if you blow on it, it flies away.

Her dad made a soft snowball and threw it at her brother, who stayed very serious for a second… and then giggled so much that he fell on his bottom.

The teacher came out in his slippers. The lady from the post office danced all by herself.

And Grandpa, who almost never ran, raced across the square, just to leave footprints.

"We have to make a snowman," said Amira.

The trouble was, there wasn't much snow. So the whole village helped. They gathered the snow from the ground, from the benches and from the edge of the well, and carried it to the middle of the square, as if they were carrying treasure on a plate.

The snowman only came up to their knees. He was small, round and a little bit crooked.

They gave him two coffee beans for eyes and a dried chilli for a nose. Grandpa tied his own stripy scarf around him.

"What's his name?" asked Amira's brother.

"Copito," said Amira.

When the snow stopped falling, the clouds opened up, and the stars came out, clean as if they'd just been washed.

That was when Amira looked at the old people of the village.

Don Efraín, who was ninety-two and had a wooden walking stick, stood in the middle of the square with his hands open. Tears were rolling down his face.

"A whole life waiting for this," he kept saying quietly. "A whole life."

And Grandpa Simón's eyes were shining.

"My grandma was right," he said. "It's exactly like this."

Amira took his hand. It was cold on the outside and warm on the inside, like all grandpas' hands.

After a while, behind the hills, the sun came up. And the sun, who knew nothing about legends, began to melt the snow.

Drops began to fall from the rooftops. Plip.

Copito grew thinner and thinner. He leaned over to one side. And in the end, all that was left were two coffee beans, a dried chilli and the stripy scarf, soaking wet.

"I don't want him to go," said Amira, and her voice wobbled.

Grandpa crouched down to her height.

"Lovely things don't have to last to be lovely," he said. "The snow has gone, yes. But you saw it. It's tucked away in here now, and nobody can melt it.

"My grandma kept her snowfall for a hundred years. You'll keep yours. And one day you'll tell it to someone small."

They walked home slowly, hand in hand, splashing in puddles on purpose. Mum made hot chocolate.

And Amira fell asleep when it was already daytime, hugging the memory of the night it snowed in the desert.
